Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verses 7–9:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses﴾ There are three opinions concerning this.

The first: it was inspiration (ilham), said by Ibn Abbas. The second: Jibril came to her with this, said by Muqatil. The third: it was a dream-vision, related by al-Mawardi. Muqatil said: the name of the mother of Moses was "Yukhabidh."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Suckle him﴾ The exegetes said: she was a midwife, a close friend of the mother of Moses. When she gave birth, the midwife took charge of her affairs, then went out, and some of the spies saw her. They came to enter upon the mother of Moses, and his sister said: "O mother, these guards are at the door." So she wrapped Moses in a cloth and placed him in the oven while it was being heated. They entered, then came out, and he said to his sister: "Where is the boy?" She said: "I do not know." Then she heard his crying from the oven and looked, and God had made the fire cool and safe for him. So she suckled him after his birth for three months, and it was said four months. When she feared for him, she made the chest (tabut) for him.

Regarding His saying: ﴿When you fear for him﴾ there are two opinions.

One: if you fear for him being killed, said by Muqatil.

The second: if you fear that he will cry out or weep so that his voice is heard, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And do not fear﴾ there are two opinions.

The first: that he will drown, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The second: that he will be lost, said by Muqatil.

Al-Asma'i said: I said to a Bedouin woman, "How eloquent you are!" She said: "Is there eloquence after this verse, which is His saying: ﴿And We revealed to the mother of Moses: Suckle him, and when you fear for him, cast him into the river, and do not fear nor grieve; We will return him to you and make him one of the messengers﴾? It combines in it two commands, two prohibitions, two reports, and two glad tidings!"

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then the family of Pharaoh picked him up﴾ Al-iltiqat (picking up) is coming upon a thing without seeking it. By "the family of Pharaoh" is meant those who undertook taking the chest from the sea.

Regarding those who picked him up there are three opinions.

The first: the maidservants of Pharaoh's wife, said by al-Suddi. The second: the daughter of Pharaoh, said by Muhammad ibn Qays. The third: the helpers of Pharaoh, said by Ibn Ishaq.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That he might become for them an enemy﴾ That is, so that the matter would end up with them being in that state, not that they took him for this purpose. This lam is called lam al-aqibah (the lam of consequence), and we have explained it in (Yunus: 88).

The exegetes have two opinions regarding the meaning of the statement.

The first: that he would be an enemy to them in their religion and a source of grief over what he would do to them.

The second: that he would be an enemy to their men and a grief concerning their women, for the men were killed by drowning and the women were enslaved. ﴿And the wife of Pharaoh said﴾ She was Asiyah daughter of Muzahim, and she was from the Children of Israel, whom Pharaoh had married: ﴿A comfort of the eye﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "Qurratu 'ayn" is in the nominative by the implied "huwa" (he is). The exegetes said: Pharaoh had only daughters born to him, so she said: ﴿Perhaps he will benefit us﴾ and we obtain good from him, ﴿or we may take him as a son﴾, ﴿while they do not perceive﴾. Concerning this there are four opinions.

The first: they do not perceive that he is an enemy to them, said by Mujahid. The second: that their destruction would be at his hands, said by Qatadah. The third: the Children of Israel do not perceive that we picked him up, said by Muhammad ibn Qays. The fourth: they do not perceive that I do what I will, not what they will, said by Muhammad ibn Ishaq.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verses 10–13:

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 14–17:

(p-207) ﴿When he reached his full strength﴾: We have explained this verse in the commentary on Surah Yusuf (12:22), and the words of the exegetes concerning the wording of the two verses are close, except that they distinguished between reaching full strength (bulugh al-ashudd) and maturity (al-istiwa'). As for reaching full strength, its explanation has already passed (6:152).

Regarding the period of maturity (al-istiwa') for them, there are two opinions.

One of them: it is forty years. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

The second: it is sixty years. This was mentioned by Ibn Jarir. The exegetes said: he remained with his mother until she weaned him, then she returned him to them, and he grew up in the care of Pharaoh and his wife, who adopted him as a son.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And he entered the city﴾. Concerning it there are two opinions.

One of them: it is Egypt. The second: it is a city near Egypt.

Al-Suddi said: Pharaoh rode out one day while Musa was not with him. When Musa came, he rode after him and caught up with him at the midday rest in that city. Others said: when Pharaoh suspected that Musa was his enemy, he ordered that he be expelled from his city, and he did not enter it except after he had grown up, so he entered it one day ﴿at a time of heedlessness of its people﴾.

(p-208) At that time there are four opinions.

The first: it was a day of festivity for them, and they had occupied themselves in it with their amusements. This was said by Ali, peace be upon him.

The second: he entered at midday. This was narrated by a group from Ibn Abbas, and Sa'id ibn Jubayr said likewise.

The third: between Maghrib and 'Isha'. This was said by Wahb ibn Munabbih.

The fourth: when they expelled him, he did not enter upon them until he had grown up, so he entered at a time when they had forgotten about him, because they had forgotten his matter. This was said by Ibn Zayd.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿This is of his faction﴾, that is, of his companions from the Children of Israel, ﴿and this is of his enemy﴾, that is, of his enemies from the Copts. The word "enemy" is used for both the singular and the plural. Al-Zajjaj said: "this" and "this" were said of the absent one as a manner of narrating as if present; the meaning is that when the observer looks at the two of them, he says: this is of his faction, and this is of his enemy. The exegetes said: the Copt had conscripted the Israelite to carry firewood to Pharaoh's kitchen. ﴿So he sought his help﴾, that is, he sought his support, ﴿and Musa struck him﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: al-wakz is to strike him with the whole palm. Ibn Qutaybah said: "fa-wakazahu" means "la-kazahu"; it is said wakaztuhu, lakaztuhu and lahaztuhu, meaning I pushed him. ﴿And he dispatched him﴾, that is, he killed him; for everything you finish with, you have qadaytahu and qadayta 'alayhi. The exegetes differ concerning what he struck him with, and there are two opinions.

One: his palm, said by Mujahid. The second: his staff, said by Qatadah.

When the Copt died, Musa regretted it, because he had not intended to kill him, and he ﴿said: this is of the work of Satan﴾, that is, it is he who stirred up my anger until I struck this man. ﴿Indeed, he is an enemy﴾ (p-209) to the son of Adam, ﴿misleading﴾ him, ﴿clearly﴾ manifest in his enmity. Then he sought forgiveness, so he ﴿said: My Lord, indeed I have wronged myself﴾, that is, by killing this man, and it is not fitting for a prophet to kill until he is commanded. ﴿He said: My Lord, by what You have bestowed upon me﴾ of forgiveness, ﴿I will never be a supporter of the criminals.﴾ Ibn Abbas said: a helper to the disbelievers. This indicates that the Israelite whom Musa helped was a disbeliever.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-wakz is to strike him with the whole palm. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 14–17:

(p-207) ﴿When he reached his full strength﴾: We have explained this verse in the commentary on Surah Yusuf (12:22), and the words of the exegetes concerning the wording of the two verses are close, except that they distinguished between reaching full strength (bulugh al-ashudd) and maturity (al-istiwa'). One of them: it is forty years. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verses 18–20:

Allah's words: ﴿So he woke up in the city, fearful, watchful﴾. It is the city in which the Egyptian was killed. ﴿Fearful﴾ for his own self, ﴿watchful﴾, i.e., awaiting harm that might befall him from them and fearing that he might be killed in return for him. ﴿Then behold, the one who had sought his help the day before﴾, who was the Israelite, ﴿was crying out to him for help﴾, i.e., seeking aid from him against another Egyptian who wanted to press him into service as well. ﴿Moses said to him﴾. Regarding the pronoun of address (ha' al-kinaya) there are two opinions.

The first: it refers to the Egyptian. The second: it refers to the Israelite, and this is the more sound view.

On the first view, the meaning is: ﴿Indeed, you are clearly misguided﴾ through your enslaving and your oppression.

On the second view there are two opinions.

The first: al-ghawiyy has the sense of al-mughwi (the one who misleads), like al-alim and al-wajih in the sense of al-mu'lim (the one who pains) and al-mu'jih (the one who wounds). The meaning is: "You are indeed a misleader, for yesterday you killed a man because of you, and today you call me to another."

The second: al-ghawiyy has the sense of al-ghawi (the one who errs). The meaning is: "You are indeed in error in fighting one whose evil you cannot ward off from yourself."

Allah's words: ﴿So when he intended to strike the one who was an enemy to both of them﴾, i.e., the Egyptian, ﴿he said, "O Moses, do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday? You only intend to be a tyrant in the land, and you do not intend to be among the reformers."﴾ This is the speech of the Israelite, with no disagreement among the exegetes that we know of. They said: When the Israelite saw Moses' anger at him when he said [to him], ﴿Indeed, you are clearly misguided﴾, and saw that he was about to strike the Pharaonic man, he thought that Moses meant him, so he feared for his own self and said, ﴿O Moses, do you intend to kill me?﴾ The people of Pharaoh had not known who killed the Egyptian, but they came to Pharaoh and said: "The Children of Israel have killed a man of ours, so take our right for us." He said: "Find for me his killer, and whoever testifies against him, and I will take your right for you." While they were going around not knowing who the killer was, this dispute occurred between the Israelite and the Egyptian on the second day. When the Israelite said to Moses, ﴿Do you intend to kill me as you killed a person yesterday?﴾, the Egyptian went off to Pharaoh and informed him that Moses was the one who had killed the man. So he ordered that Moses be killed. A man from Moses' party learned of this and came to him and informed him. That is His saying: ﴿And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running﴾.

As for al-jabbar (the tyrant), al-Suddi said: it is the killing. We have explained it in (Hud: 59). Aqsa al-madina is its farthest and most distant part. Yas'a means yusri' (hastens). Ibn Abbas said: this man was the believer of Pharaoh's family, and the disagreement about his name will come in surah (al-Mu'minun: 28). As for al-mala', they are the notables and the nobles of the people.

Regarding His saying ﴿conspire against you﴾ (ya'tamirun bika) there are three opinions.

The first: they consult about you in order to kill you, said by Abu Ubayda. The second: they resolve upon you, said by Ibn Qutayba. The third: some of them order others to kill you, said by al-Zajjaj.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 28, verses 21–28:**

[p. 212]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So he left from it﴾, that is, from Egypt, ﴿fearful﴾. Its explanation has already passed [al-Qasas: 18].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Save me from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning the polytheists, the people of Egypt.

﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, facing Madyan and its direction. Its root is *al-liqa'* (meeting), and a *ta'* was added to it. The poet said:

*I hoped for your bounty, will its promises come true?*
*But today hope has fallen short of reaching your *tilqa'* (presence).*

That is, of your *liqa'* (meeting).

The commentators said: He left in fear, without provisions or a mount, and the distance between Egypt and Madyan was eight days' journey. He had no knowledge of the road. So ﴿he said: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way"﴾, that is, to his destination. Ibn 'Abbas said: He had no knowledge of the road except his good opinion of his Lord. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent an angel to him, and he guided him. They said: He had no food on his way except the leaves of trees, and when he reached the water of Madyan, the greenness of the herbs was visible through his belly because of his emaciation.

The *ummah* (community) is the group, and they were shepherds, ﴿watering﴾ their livestock. ﴿And he found besides them﴾, that is, besides the group, ﴿two women﴾, and they were the two daughters of Shu'ayb. Muqatil said: The name of the elder was Safura and the younger was 'Ibra. ﴿Holding back﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, they were keeping back their sheep, so he omitted "the sheep" for brevity. The commentators said: They only did that so that the people would finish and the well would be clear for them. Musa said: ﴿What is your business?﴾, that is, what is your matter, that you do not water? ﴿They said: "We cannot water until the shepherds finish"﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Jawza', Ibn Ya'mur, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *nusqi* with a *damma* on the *nun*. ﴿Until the shepherds leave [yusdiru]﴾. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Ja'far read *yasdaru* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *dal*, meaning: until the shepherds return. The rest read *yusdiru* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *dal*, meaning: until the shepherds bring their flocks away from the water. *Al-ri'a'* is the plural of *ra'in* (shepherd), as one says *sahib* and *sihab* (companion, companions). 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Ya'mur, and 'Asim al-Jahdari read *al-ru'a'* with a *damma* on the *ra'*. The meaning is: We are two women and cannot compete with the men. ﴿And our father is an old man﴾ who cannot water his livestock because of his age. Therefore we had to water them. There was a great rock over that well. When the shepherds finished watering, they replaced the rock, so the two women came to the leftover water of the shepherds' troughs and watered their sheep. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, that is, Musa.

There are two views about what he did.

The first: He went to another well over which there was a rock that only a group of people could lift. He lifted it and watered for them. This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Shurayh.

The second: He pushed through the people for the water and watered for them. This was said by Ibn Ishaq, and the meaning is: he watered their sheep for their sake.

﴿Then he turned back﴾, that is, he withdrew, ﴿to the shade﴾, which was the shade of a tree. ﴿And he said: "My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me"﴾. The *lam* here means *ila* (to), so the sense is: I am in need of what You send down to me of good. By "good" he meant food. Ibn Jarir reported that he made the two women hear these words as a hint that they should feed him.

﴿Then one of them came to him﴾. The meaning is: When their sheep had drunk, they returned to their father and told him the story of Musa. So he sent one of them to call Musa. There are two views about who she was: the younger, or the elder. ﴿She came to him walking shyly﴾, having covered her face with the sleeve of her garment.

There are three views about the cause of her shyness:

First: It was one of her traits to be modest, so she walked like one who was not accustomed to going out and coming in.

Second: Because she had invited him so that he would reward her, and it was more becoming in her eyes to invite him without a reward.

Third: Because she was her father's messenger.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That he may reward you for what you watered for us﴾. The commentators said: When Musa heard this, he disliked it and wanted not to follow her. But he had no choice because of the hardship he was in, so he followed her. The wind was blowing her garment against her, so that it showed some of her body. He called to her: "O servant of Allah, walk behind me and direct me on the way."

﴿So when he came to him﴾, that is, when Musa came to Shu'ayb, ﴿and related to him the story﴾, that is, he told him his affair from the time he was born and the reason that drove him out of his land. ﴿He said: "Fear not. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people"﴾, that is, Pharaoh has no authority in our land, and we are not in his kingdom.

﴿One of the two women said﴾, and she was the elder: ﴿"O father, hire him, for the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy"﴾, that is, the best of those you employ for your work is the one who is strong for your work and fulfills trust. She called him strong because he lifted the rock from the top of the well. It was said: because he drew water with a bucket that only a large number of men could lift. She called him trustworthy because he told her to walk behind him. Al-Suddi said: Shu'ayb said to her: "I have seen his strength, but how do you know of his trustworthiness?" So she told him.

The commentators said: Shu'ayb was pleased with him and said to him: ﴿"I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years"﴾. Al-Farra' said: *tu'jurani* and *tu'jirani* (you hire me), with a *damma* or *kasra* on the *jim*, are two dialects. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that you will be my hired worker for eight years. ﴿And if you complete ten, it will be of your own accord﴾, that is, that is an act of grace from you, and it is not obligatory upon you.

Fourth: He was Yathrun, the son of Shu'ayb's brother. This was narrated by 'Amr ibn Murrah from Abu 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn al-Sa'ib also said so.

They differed about which of the two daughters Musa married, in two views.

First: The younger. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Second: The elder. This was said by Muqatil.

First: Safuriya, related by Abu 'Imran al-Jawni. Second: Safura, said by Shu'ayb al-Jibba'i. Third: Sabura, said by Muqatil.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 28, verses 21–28:**

[p. 212]

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿So he left from it﴾, that is, from Egypt, ﴿fearful﴾. Its explanation has already passed [al-Qasas: 18].

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Save me from the wrongdoing people﴾, meaning the polytheists, the people of Egypt.

﴿And when he turned toward Madyan﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, facing Madyan and its direction. Its root is *al-liqa'* (meeting), and a *ta'* was added to it. The poet said:

*I hoped for your bounty, will its promises come true?*
*But today hope has fallen short of reaching your *tilqa'* (presence).*

That is, of your *liqa'* (meeting).

The commentators said: He left in fear, without provisions or a mount, and the distance between Egypt and Madyan was eight days' journey. He had no knowledge of the road. So ﴿he said: "Perhaps my Lord will guide me to the right way"﴾, that is, to his destination. Ibn 'Abbas said: He had no knowledge of the road except his good opinion of his Lord. Al-Suddi said: Allah sent an angel to him, and he guided him. They said: He had no food on his way except the leaves of trees, and when he reached the water of Madyan, the greenness of the herbs was visible through his belly because of his emaciation.

The *ummah* (community) is the group, and they were shepherds, ﴿watering﴾ their livestock. ﴿And he found besides them﴾, that is, besides the group, ﴿two women﴾, and they were the two daughters of Shu'ayb. Muqatil said: The name of the elder was Safura and the younger was 'Ibra. ﴿Holding back﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: That is, they were keeping back their sheep, so he omitted "the sheep" for brevity. The commentators said: They only did that so that the people would finish and the well would be clear for them. Musa said: ﴿What is your business?﴾, that is, what is your matter, that you do not water? ﴿They said: "We cannot water until the shepherds finish"﴾. Ibn Mas'ud, Abu al-Jawza', Ibn Ya'mur, and Ibn al-Sumayfa' read *nusqi* with a *damma* on the *nun*. ﴿Until the shepherds leave [yusdiru]﴾. Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Abu Ja'far read *yasdaru* with a *fatha* on the *ya'* and a *damma* on the *dal*, meaning: until the shepherds return. The rest read *yusdiru* with a *damma* on the *ya'* and a *kasra* on the *dal*, meaning: until the shepherds bring their flocks away from the water. *Al-ri'a'* is the plural of *ra'in* (shepherd), as one says *sahib* and *sihab* (companion, companions). 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn Ya'mur, and 'Asim al-Jahdari read *al-ru'a'* with a *damma* on the *ra'*. The meaning is: We are two women and cannot compete with the men. ﴿And our father is an old man﴾ who cannot water his livestock because of his age. Therefore we had to water them. There was a great rock over that well. When the shepherds finished watering, they replaced the rock, so the two women came to the leftover water of the shepherds' troughs and watered their sheep. ﴿So he watered for them﴾, that is, Musa.

There are two views about what he did.

The first: He went to another well over which there was a rock that only a group of people could lift. He lifted it and watered for them. This was said by 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and Shurayh.

The second: He pushed through the people for the water and watered for them. This was said by Ibn Ishaq, and the meaning is: he watered their sheep for their sake.

﴿Then he turned back﴾, that is, he withdrew, ﴿to the shade﴾, which was the shade of a tree. ﴿And he said: "My Lord, I am in need of whatever good You send down to me"﴾. The *lam* here means *ila* (to), so the sense is: I am in need of what You send down to me of good. By "good" he meant food. Ibn Jarir reported that he made the two women hear these words as a hint that they should feed him.

﴿Then one of them came to him﴾. The meaning is: When their sheep had drunk, they returned to their father and told him the story of Musa. So he sent one of them to call Musa. There are two views about who she was: the younger, or the elder. ﴿She came to him walking shyly﴾, having covered her face with the sleeve of her garment.

There are three views about the cause of her shyness:

First: It was one of her traits to be modest, so she walked like one who was not accustomed to going out and coming in.

Second: Because she had invited him so that he would reward her, and it was more becoming in her eyes to invite him without a reward.

Third: Because she was her father's messenger.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That he may reward you for what you watered for us﴾. The commentators said: When Musa heard this, he disliked it and wanted not to follow her. But he had no choice because of the hardship he was in, so he followed her. The wind was blowing her garment against her, so that it showed some of her body. He called to her: "O servant of Allah, walk behind me and direct me on the way."

﴿So when he came to him﴾, that is, when Musa came to Shu'ayb, ﴿and related to him the story﴾, that is, he told him his affair from the time he was born and the reason that drove him out of his land. ﴿He said: "Fear not. You have escaped from the wrongdoing people"﴾, that is, Pharaoh has no authority in our land, and we are not in his kingdom.

﴿One of the two women said﴾, and she was the elder: ﴿"O father, hire him, for the best one you can hire is the strong and trustworthy"﴾, that is, the best of those you employ for your work is the one who is strong for your work and fulfills trust. She called him strong because he lifted the rock from the top of the well. It was said: because he drew water with a bucket that only a large number of men could lift. She called him trustworthy because he told her to walk behind him. Al-Suddi said: Shu'ayb said to her: "I have seen his strength, but how do you know of his trustworthiness?" So she told him.

The commentators said: Shu'ayb was pleased with him and said to him: ﴿"I wish to marry you to one of these two daughters of mine, on condition that you serve me for eight years"﴾. Al-Farra' said: *tu'jurani* and *tu'jirani* (you hire me), with a *damma* or *kasra* on the *jim*, are two dialects. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is that you will be my hired worker for eight years. ﴿And if you complete ten, it will be of your own accord﴾, that is, that is an act of grace from you, and it is not obligatory upon you.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And I do not wish to burden you﴾, that is, in the ten years, ﴿you will find me, if Allah wills, among the righteous﴾, that is, in good companionship and fulfilling what you have said.

﴿He said﴾, that is, Musa said to him: ﴿"That is between me and you"﴾, that is, whatever you have described and stipulated for me, that is for you, and whatever you have stipulated for me of marrying one of them, that is for me. The matter is thus between us. The speech ends here. Then he said: ﴿"Whichever of the two terms I fulfill"﴾, meaning the eight or the ten. Abu 'Ubayda said: *ma* is superfluous here.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿"Whichever I complete"﴾, that is, I fulfill it. ﴿"Then there shall be no transgression against me"﴾, that is, there is no way against me. The meaning is: Do not be unjust to me by obliging me to more than that. ﴿"And Allah is Guardian over what we say"﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, Allah is our witness to what some of us have agreed with others.

First: He was Shu'ayb, the Prophet of Allah (ﷺ). This is the view of most of the exegetes, and there is a report from the Prophet (ﷺ) indicating it. Wahb and Muqatil also said so.

Second: He was the ruler of Madyan, whose name was Yathra. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Third: He was a man from the people of Shu'ayb. This was said by al-Hasan.

Fourth: He was Yathrun, the son of Shu'ayb's brother. This was narrated by 'Amr ibn Murrah from Abu 'Ubayda ibn 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud, and Ibn al-Sa'ib also said so.

First: The younger. This was reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Second: The elder. This was said by Muqatil.

First: Safuriya, related by Abu 'Imran al-Jawni. Second: Safura, said by Shu'ayb al-Jibba'i. Third: Sabura, said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 29–35:

Allah's words: ﴿When Musa had fulfilled the term﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, related that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked which of the two terms Musa fulfilled, and he said: "The more complete and the better of the two." Mujahid said: he remained with them ten more years after fulfilling the term. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: he stayed with them for years after he had brought his wife in to him. The tafsir of this verse has already been covered [Ta-Ha: 10] up to His words: ﴿or a brand﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi, Abu ʿAmr, Ibn ʿAmir and al-Kisa'i read "jidhwatan" with a kasra on the jim. ʿAsim read it with a fatha. Hamza, Khalaf and al-Walid, on the authority of Ibn ʿAmir, read it with a damma. All of these are dialectal variants (lughat). Ibn ʿAbbas said: al-jadhwah is a piece of wood in which there is fire. Abu ʿUbayda said: it is a thick piece of wood with no flame, and it is like the stump (al-jidhmah) from the root of a tree. Ibn Muqbil said:

Layla's gatherers of firewood spent the night seeking for her
sturdy branches, neither soft nor rotten.

Al-daʿr is that which has become rotten, and from it comes "rajul dāʿir," meaning corrupt.

Allah's words: ﴿He was called from the right side of the valley﴾, that is, its side, ﴿on the right﴾, which is on the right of Musa, ﴿in the blessed plot﴾, which is a piece of land, ﴿from the tree﴾ with Allah speaking to Musa there. That is, from its direction. Regarding that tree there are two views.

One: it is the jujube tree (shajarat al-unnab), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: it is a thornbush (ʿawsaja), said by Qatada, Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

What follows has already been explained [an-Naml: 10] up to His words: ﴿that you are among the secure﴾, that is, from anything disagreeable reaching you.

Allah's words: ﴿Insert your hand﴾, that is, put it in, ﴿and draw your arm to your side﴾. We have explained the janah (wing/arm) in (Ta-Ha: 22), except that some exegetes differed between the explanations of the two expressions, so we explained it. Ibn Zayd said: its janah is the forearm, the upper arm and the palm. Al-Zajjaj said: the janah here is the upper arm, and the whole hand is also called janah. Ibn al-Anbari reported from al-Farra' that he said: the janah here is the staff. Ibn al-Anbari said: the janah of a human is likened to the wing of a bird. In one usage the Arabs liken a person's legs to the two wings of a bird, so they say: "So-and-so has passed by, flying on his two wings," meaning running on his two feet. In another usage they treat the upper arm as the wing of a bird, as in His words: ﴿and draw your hand to your wing﴾. In another usage they treat the staff as the wing, because a person pushes away from himself with it as a bird pushes away with its wing, as in His words: ﴿and draw your arm to your side from fear﴾. The term "wing" is applied to these things only by way of likeness and metaphor, as one says: "His wing has been clipped," and "his hand and foot have been cut off" when a calamity strikes and nullifies his actions; and a man says to another: "You are my hand and my foot," meaning: you are the one through whom I reach what I love. Jarir said:

I will thank her for returning my feathers to me and for growing the primary feathers back on my wing.

A woman of the Arabs lamented her husband, al-Aghharr, saying:

O my protection in calamities, and O my pillar, and O my right hand.
May I never be shielded, I who used to shield your face,
while your face decays in the dust.

As for "al-rahb," Ibn Kathir, Nafi and Abu ʿAmr read "min al-rahab" with a fatha on the ra' and the ha'. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "min al-ruhb" with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the ha'. Hafs and Aban, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "min al-rahb" with a fatha on the ra' and a sukun on the ha' (this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ). Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan and Qatada read it with a damma on both the ra' and the ha'. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ruhb and al-rahab have the same meaning, like al-rushd and al-rashad. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-ruhb and al-rahbah both mean fear and dread. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-rahb, al-ruhub and al-rahab are like al-shaghl, al-shughul and al-shaghal, and al-bakhl, al-bukhul and al-bakhal; these are dialects that return to the meaning of fear and dread.

There are three views among the exegetes on the meaning of this verse.

One: when he fled from the serpent, Allah commanded him to draw his arm to himself so that fright would leave him. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is, "Draw your hand to your chest out of fear, and there is no fear for you." Mujahid said: whoever is frightened and draws his arm to himself, the fright leaves him.

The second: when the whiteness of his hand and its radiance dismayed him, he was commanded to put it into his collar, and it returned to its original state.

The third: the meaning of the speech is: "Let your dread be calmed and your heart be steadied." Abu ʿAli said: it does not mean joining two things together; rather it is a command to resolve upon what he was commanded and to strive in it, similar to His words: "Gird up your loins for death."

Allah's words: ﴿These two are two proofs﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "fa-dhanika" with shadda. The rest read "fa-dhanika" with no shadda. Al-Zajjaj said: the shadda is the dual of "dhalika," and the lightened form is the dual of "dhaka," so the lam in "dhalika" replaces the shadda of the nun in "dhanika." ﴿Two proofs﴾, that is, two clear demonstrations. The exegetes said: "these two" refers to the staff and the hand, two proofs from Allah for Musa's truthfulness, ﴿sent to Pharaoh﴾, that is, We sent with these two signs to Pharaoh. The tafsir of what follows [ash-Shuʿara: 14] has already been covered up to His words: ﴿he is more eloquent in tongue than I﴾, that is, better in expression, because there remained in Musa's tongue the effect of the ember he had taken up. ﴿So send him with me as a helper﴾. Most readers read "ridan" with a sukun on the dal and a hamza after it. Abu Jaʿfar read "raddan" with a fatha on the dal and an alif after it, without tanwin or hamza. Nafi read it the same way except that he added tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: al-radhu means help; it is said: "radhatuhu aradhuhu radhan," meaning: when I helped him.

Allah's words: ﴿to confirm me﴾. ʿAsim and Hamza read "yusaddiqunī" with a damma on the qaf. The rest read it with a sukun on the qaf. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "yusaddiq" with a jazm takes it as an answer to the request: "Send him, he will confirm me." Whoever reads it with a raf' means: a helper confirming me. Most exegetes hold that by "yusaddiqunī" he pointed to Harun. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: so that Pharaoh may believe me.

Allah's words: ﴿We will strengthen your arm with your brother﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "We will assist you with your brother," and the word "arm" is used as a figure, because the strength of the hand lies in its arm, and everything that supports is an arm. ﴿And We will give you both authority﴾, that is, a clear proof. It is said that "salit" is oil, because it is used for light; and "sultan" is the clearest proof.

Allah's words: ﴿so they will not reach you﴾, that is, with killing or harm.

Regarding His words: ﴿by Our signs﴾ there are three views.

One: the meaning is that you two are protected from them by Our signs and proofs, so they cannot reach you.

The second: it is connected to what follows, so the meaning is: by Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victorious, that is, you will prevail by Our signs.

The third: there is inversion in the speech, its implied sense being: "We will give you both authority by Our signs, so they will not reach you."

Ibn Zayd said: its janah is the forearm, the upper arm and the palm. Al-Zajjaj said: the janah here is the upper arm, and the whole hand is also called janah. Ibn al-Anbari reported from al-Farra' that he said: the janah here is the staff. Ibn al-Anbari said: the janah of a human is likened to the wing of a bird. In one usage the Arabs liken a person's legs to the two wings of a bird, so they say: "So-and-so has passed by, flying on his two wings," meaning running on his two feet. In another usage they treat the upper arm as the wing of a bird, as in His words: ﴿and draw your hand to your wing﴾. In another usage they treat the staff as the wing, because a person pushes away from himself with it as a bird pushes away with its wing, as in His words: ﴿and draw your arm to your side from fear﴾. The term "wing" is applied to these things only by way of likeness and metaphor, as one says: "His wing has been clipped," and "his hand and foot have been cut off" when a calamity strikes and nullifies his actions; and a man says to another: "You are my hand and my foot," meaning: you are the one through whom I reach what I love. Jarir said:

I will thank her for returning my feathers to me and for growing the primary feathers back on my wing.

A woman of the Arabs lamented her husband, al-Aghharr, saying:

O my protection in calamities, and O my pillar, and O my right hand.
May I never be shielded, I who used to shield your face,
while your face decays in the dust.

As for "al-rahb," Ibn Kathir, Nafi and Abu ʿAmr read "min al-rahab" with a fatha on the ra' and the ha'. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "min al-ruhb" with a damma on the ra' and a sukun on the ha'. Hafs and Aban, on the authority of ʿAsim, read "min al-rahb" with a fatha on the ra' and a sukun on the ha' (this is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibn al-Sumayfaʿ). Ubayy ibn Kaʿb, al-Hasan and Qatada read it with a damma on both the ra' and the ha'. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ruhb and al-rahab have the same meaning, like al-rushd and al-rashad. Abu ʿUbayda said: al-ruhb and al-rahbah both mean fear and dread. Ibn al-Anbari said: al-rahb, al-ruhub and al-rahab are like al-shaghl, al-shughul and al-shaghal, and al-bakhl, al-bukhul and al-bakhal; these are dialects that return to the meaning of fear and dread.

There are three views among the exegetes on the meaning of this verse.

One: when he fled from the serpent, Allah commanded him to draw his arm to himself so that fright would leave him. Ibn ʿAbbas said: the meaning is, "Draw your hand to your chest out of fear, and there is no fear for you." Mujahid said: whoever is frightened and draws his arm to himself, the fright leaves him.

The second: when the whiteness of his hand and its radiance dismayed him, he was commanded to put it into his collar, and it returned to its original state.

The third: the meaning of the speech is: "Let your dread be calmed and your heart be steadied." Abu ʿAli said: it does not mean joining two things together; rather it is a command to resolve upon what he was commanded and to strive in it, similar to His words: "Gird up your loins for death."

Allah's words: ﴿These two are two proofs﴾. Ibn Kathir and Abu ʿAmr read "fa-dhanika" with shadda. The rest read "fa-dhanika" with no shadda. Al-Zajjaj said: the shadda is the dual of "dhalika," and the lightened form is the dual of "dhaka," so the lam in "dhalika" replaces the shadda of the nun in "dhanika." ﴿Two proofs﴾, that is, two clear demonstrations. The exegetes said: "these two" refers to the staff and the hand, two proofs from Allah for Musa's truthfulness, ﴿sent to Pharaoh﴾, that is, We sent with these two signs to Pharaoh. The tafsir of what follows [ash-Shuʿara: 14] has already been covered up to His words: ﴿he is more eloquent in tongue than I﴾, that is, better in expression, because there remained in Musa's tongue the effect of the ember he had taken up. ﴿So send him with me as a helper﴾. Most readers read "ridan" with a sukun on the dal and a hamza after it. Abu Jaʿfar read "raddan" with a fatha on the dal and an alif after it, without tanwin or hamza. Nafi read it the same way except that he added tanwin. Al-Zajjaj said: al-radhu means help; it is said: "radhatuhu aradhuhu radhan," meaning: when I helped him.

Allah's words: ﴿to confirm me﴾. ʿAsim and Hamza read "yusaddiqunī" with a damma on the qaf. The rest read it with a sukun on the qaf. Al-Zajjaj said: whoever reads "yusaddiq" with a jazm takes it as an answer to the request: "Send him, he will confirm me." Whoever reads it with a raf' means: a helper confirming me. Most exegetes hold that by "yusaddiqunī" he pointed to Harun. Muqatil ibn Sulayman said: so that Pharaoh may believe me.

Allah's words: ﴿We will strengthen your arm with your brother﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is, "We will assist you with your brother," and the word "arm" is used as a figure, because the strength of the hand lies in its arm, and everything that supports is an arm. ﴿And We will give you both authority﴾, that is, a clear proof. It is said that "salit" is oil, because it is used for light; and "sultan" is the clearest proof.

Allah's words: ﴿so they will not reach you﴾, that is, with killing or harm.

Regarding His words: ﴿by Our signs﴾ there are three views.

One: the meaning is that you two are protected from them by Our signs and proofs, so they cannot reach you.

The second: it is connected to what follows, so the meaning is: by Our signs, you and those who follow you will be the victorious, that is, you will prevail by Our signs.

The third: there is inversion in the speech, its implied sense being: "We will give you both authority by Our signs, so they will not reach you."

One: it is the jujube tree (shajarat al-unnab), said by Ibn ʿAbbas.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 38–42:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O Haman, kindle for me [a fire] upon the clay﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is, make for me bricks (ājurr). ﴿Then make for me a lofty tower (ṣarḥ)﴾, that is, a high palace. Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṣarḥ is every building that is spacious and elevated. It is related in the tafsir that when he (Pharaoh) commanded Haman, his minister, to build the tower, he gathered the workers and craftsmen until there assembled fifty thousand builders, besides the followers. They raised it and built it up until it rose to a height that no one's building had ever reached. When it was completed, Pharaoh climbed atop it and ordered an arrow shot toward the sky. It was returned to him smeared with blood, and he said: "I have killed the god of Moses." Then God Almighty sent Gabriel, who struck it with his wing and cut it into three pieces. One piece fell upon Pharaoh's army and killed a million men, one piece fell into the sea, and another fell in the west.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That I may look upon the God of Moses﴾, that is, that I may ascend to Him and look down upon Him. ﴿And indeed I think him﴾, meaning Moses, ﴿to be among the liars﴾ in his claim of a god other than me. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: I think Moses is lying in his claim that there is a Lord in the sky whom he has sent. ﴿And he and his soldiers were arrogant in the land﴾, meaning the land of Egypt, ﴿without right﴾, that is, through falsehood and wrongdoing. ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ for the Resurrection and recompense. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yurja'ūn" with a raised yā'; Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatḥah on it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made them﴾, that is, in this world, ﴿leaders (a'immah)﴾, that is, leaders in disbelief whom the tyrants follow, ﴿calling to the Fire﴾, because whoever obeys them enters it. And "they will not be helped" means: they will not be protected from the punishment. What follows this has been explained in (Hud: 60, 99).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Of those who are disfigured (al-maqbūḥīn)﴾, that is, of those who are distanced and cursed. Abu Zayd said: it is said, "God disfigured so-and-so," meaning He distanced him from every good. Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of the verse is: We caused a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection there is another curse; then he resumed speech and said: they are among the disfigured.

Al-Zajjaj said: al-ṣarḥ is every building that is spacious and elevated. It is related in the tafsir that when he (Pharaoh) commanded Haman, his minister, to build the tower, he gathered the workers and craftsmen until there assembled fifty thousand builders, besides the followers. They raised it and built it up until it rose to a height that no one's building had ever reached. When it was completed, Pharaoh climbed atop it and ordered an arrow shot toward the sky. It was returned to him smeared with blood, and he said: "I have killed the god of Moses." Then God Almighty sent Gabriel, who struck it with his wing and cut it into three pieces. One piece fell upon Pharaoh's army and killed a million men, one piece fell into the sea, and another fell in the west.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That I may look upon the God of Moses﴾, that is, that I may ascend to Him and look down upon Him. ﴿And indeed I think him﴾, meaning Moses, ﴿to be among the liars﴾ in his claim of a god other than me. Ibn Jarir said: the meaning is: I think Moses is lying in his claim that there is a Lord in the sky whom he has sent. ﴿And he and his soldiers were arrogant in the land﴾, meaning the land of Egypt, ﴿without right﴾, that is, through falsehood and wrongdoing. ﴿And they thought that they would not be returned to Us﴾ for the Resurrection and recompense. Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, 'Asim and Ibn 'Amir read "yurja'ūn" with a raised yā'; Nafi', Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read it with a fatḥah on it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We made them﴾, that is, in this world, ﴿leaders (a'immah)﴾, that is, leaders in disbelief whom the tyrants follow, ﴿calling to the Fire﴾, because whoever obeys them enters it. And "they will not be helped" means: they will not be protected from the punishment. What follows this has been explained in (Hud: 60, 99).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Of those who are disfigured (al-maqbūḥīn)﴾, that is, of those who are distanced and cursed. Abu Zayd said: it is said, "God disfigured so-and-so," meaning He distanced him from every good. Ibn Jurayj said: the meaning of the verse is: We caused a curse to follow them in this world, and on the Day of Resurrection there is another curse; then he resumed speech and said: they are among the disfigured.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 43–47:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿After We had destroyed the earlier generations﴾, meaning the people of Noah, ʿAd, Thamud and others, ﴿as insight for mankind﴾, that is, so that they might be shown the way by it and be guided.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And you were not on the western side﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: that is, you were not on the side of the western mountain.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿When We decreed the command to Musa﴾, that is, We settled the matter with him by sending him to Pharaoh and his people. ﴿Nor were you among the witnesses﴾ to that matter. In this there is a proof of the truth of the prophethood of our Prophet (ﷺ), for they know that he did not read the books and did not witness what took place; so had it not been revealed to him, he would not have known it.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But We brought into being generations﴾, that is, We created nations after Musa. ﴿So the lifetime grew long for them﴾, that is, their respite was prolonged, so they forgot the covenant of God and abandoned His command. This indicates that He had made covenants with Musa and his people concerning the matter of Muhammad (ﷺ), and they were commanded to believe in him; but when their respite was prolonged, they turned away from observing the covenants. ﴿Nor were you dwelling﴾, that is, residing ﴿among the people of Madyan﴾, so that you would learn the account of Musa and Shuʿayb and his two daughters and recite that to the people of Makkah. ﴿But We were sending messengers﴾: We sent you to the people of Makkah and informed you of the account of those who came before, and had it not been for that you would not have known it.

﴿Nor were you on the side of the Tur﴾, that is, on the side of the mountain upon which Musa was spoken to ﴿when We called out﴾ to Musa and spoke to him. This is the saying of the majority. Abu Hurayrah said: this call was: "O community of Muhammad, I have given you before you ask Me, and I answer you before you call upon Me."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But it is a mercy from your Lord﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: you did not witness the stories of the prophets, but We revealed them to you and related them to you, as a mercy from your Lord.

﴿And had it not been that a calamity should befall them﴾: the answer to "had it not been" (law-la) is omitted; its estimate is: had it not been that they would argue, by saying that no messenger was sent to them, We would have hastened the punishment upon them. And it was said: had it not been for that, we would not have needed to send messengers, and the argument would not have been preferred.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 48–55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But when the truth came to them from Us﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿the truth from Us﴾, which is Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the Qur'an, ﴿they said: "Why was he not given the like of what was given to Musa?"﴾ That is, "Why not (halla)," ﴿given﴾ Muhammad, ﴿of the signs, the like of what was given to Musa,﴾ such as the staff and the hand. The exegetes said: The Jews instructed the Quraysh to ask Muhammad for the like of what was given to Musa. So Allah, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Did they not disbelieve in what was given to Musa?﴾ That is, they had indeed disbelieved in the signs of Musa. As for ﴿they said﴾ concerning those being referred to, there are two views. One: the Jews. The second: the Quraysh. ﴿Two magics﴾: Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "sahiran" (two sorcerers). ﴿Supporting one another﴾ means cooperating. Al-'Abbas al-Ansari transmitted from Abu 'Amr: "tazzahara" with the letter ẓā' doubled.

Concerning whom they meant, there are three views.

One: Musa and Muhammad, said by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan and Sa'id ibn Jubayr; according to this, it is from the saying of the polytheist Arabs.

The second: Musa and Harun, said by Mujahid; according to this, it is from the saying of the Jews to them both at the beginning of the prophethood.

The third: Muhammad and 'Isa, said by Qatadah; according to this, it is from the saying of the Jews who did not believe in our Prophet.

'Asim, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "sihrani" (two magics), and concerning this there are three views.

One: the Torah and the Furqan, said by Ibn 'Abbas and al-Suddi.

The second: the Gospel and the Qur'an, said by Qatadah.

The third: the Torah and the Gospel, said by Abu Mijlaz and Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid. The meaning of the statement is: each of these two magics strengthens the other, so "supporting" is attributed to the two magics as a broadening of speech. ﴿And they said: "Indeed we are disbelievers in both."﴾ They mean what has been mentioned before, according to the differing views. So Allah said to His Prophet: ﴿Say﴾ to the disbelievers of Makkah: ﴿"Then bring a Book from Allah which is better guidance than both of them,﴾ that is, than the Torah and the Qur'an, ﴿if you are truthful"﴾ that they are two sorcerers. ﴿But if they do not respond to you﴾ meaning, if they do not bring the like of the Torah and the Qur'an, ﴿then know that they only follow their own desires﴾ meaning, that what they have embraced of disbelief was not driven by any proof, but they have preferred desire in it. ﴿And who is more astray﴾ meaning, there is no one more astray ﴿than one who follows his desire without guidance﴾ meaning, without right direction or clear evidence ﴿from Allah?﴾

﴿And We have certainly conveyed to them the word﴾. Al-Hasan, Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn Ya'mur read "wasalna" with the letter ṣād lightened.

Concerning those being referred to, there are two views.

One: that they are the Quraysh, said by most of the scholars, among them Mujahid.

The second: the Jews, said by Rifa'ah al-Qurazi.

The meaning: We sent down the Qur'an, one part following another, and it informs about the earlier nations, how they were punished, so that perhaps they would take heed.

﴿Those to whom We gave the Book﴾, and concerning them there are three views. One: that they are the believers among the People of the Book, related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid said likewise.

The second: the Muslims among the People of the Gospel. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn 'Abbas that forty of the companions of the Negus came to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and witnessed Uhud with him, so this verse was revealed concerning them.

The third: the Muslims among the Jews, such as 'Abdullah ibn Salam and others, said by al-Suddi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿before it﴾, that is, before the Qur'an, ﴿they had submitted﴾. Regarding the pronoun in "bihi" (by it/him) there are two views. One: it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, because his mention was written [among them] in their books, so they believed in him. The second: it refers to the Qur'an.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when it is recited to them﴾, meaning the Qur'an, ﴿they say: "We believe in it; indeed it is the truth from our Lord. Indeed we were submitting before it"﴾, that is, before the revelation of the Qur'an, ﴿Muslims﴾, that is, sincere to Allah, affirming Muhammad, and that is because his mention was in their books, so they believed in him. ﴿Those will be given their reward twice﴾. Concerning those being referred to, there are two views.

One: that they are the believers among the People of the Book; this is the view of the majority, and it is the apparent meaning.

Concerning what they endured patiently, there are two views. One: they were patient with the first Book, and patient in following Muhammad, said by Qatadah and Ibn Zayd. The second: they were patient in believing in Muhammad before he was sent, and then in following him when he was sent, said by al-Dahhak.

The second view: that they are a people from among the polytheists who embraced Islam, and their people used to harm them, so they bore the harm patiently, said by Mujahid.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they repel evil with good﴾. Concerning this there are sayings which we have explained in (al-Ra'd: 22).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when they hear idle talk﴾. Concerning this there are three views. One: harm and abuse, said by Mujahid. The second: polytheism, said by al-Dahhak. The third: that they are a people from among the Jews who believed, and they used to hear what the Jews had altered of the description of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, and they disliked that and turned away from it, said by Ibn Zayd. Is this abrogated or not? Concerning this there are two views.

Concerning His saying: ﴿And they say: "To us our deeds, and to you your deeds"﴾ there are two views. One: to us our religion and to you your religion. The second: to us our forbearance and to you your foolishness.

﴿Peace be upon you﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: they did not intend a greeting; rather they meant: between us and you is disengagement. This was before the Muslims were commanded to fight. The exegetes mentioned that this is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

Concerning His saying: ﴿We do not seek the ignorant﴾ there are three views. One: we do not seek the religion of the ignorant. The second: we do not seek to be their neighbours. The third: we do not want to become ignorant ourselves.

The third: Muhammad and 'Isa, said by Qatadah; according to this, it is from the saying of the Jews who did not believe in our Prophet.

One: it refers to Muhammad ﷺ, because his mention was written [among them] in their books, so they believed in him. The second: it refers to the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 56–58:

(p-231) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾. We have already mentioned its occasion of revelation at His saying: ﴿It is not for the Prophet and those who believe to ask forgiveness for the polytheists﴾ [At-Tawbah: 113]. Muslim related, in what he alone transmitted apart from al-Bukhari, from the hadith of Abu Hurayrah, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said to his uncle: 'Say: There is no god but Allah, and I will testify for you with it on the Day of Resurrection.' He said: 'Were it not that the women of Quraysh would reproach me, saying, "It was only fear that made him do it," I would have comforted your eye with it.' So Allah, Mighty and Majestic, revealed: ﴿Indeed, you do not guide whom you like﴾." Al-Zajjaj said: The exegetes agreed that it was revealed concerning Abu Talib.

(p-232) Regarding His saying ﴿whom you like﴾, there are two views:

One: whom you like to be guided. The second: whom you love because of his kinship.

﴿But Allah guides whom He wills﴾, i.e., He gives guidance to His religion to whom He wills. ﴿And He is most knowing of those who are guided﴾, i.e., of those for whom He has decreed guidance.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they say: If we follow the guidance with you﴾. Ibn Abbas, in the narration of al-Awfi, said: They were some people of Quraysh who said that. He also said, in the narration of Ibn Abi Mulaykah, that al-Harith ibn Amir ibn Nawfal said that. Muqatil mentioned that al-Harith ibn Amir said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "We know that what you say is true, but what prevents us from following the guidance [al-huda] with you is our fear that the Arabs will snatch us away from our land," meaning Makkah. The meaning of the verse is: If we follow you in your religion, we fear the Arabs because of our opposition to them. Al-takhattuf (snatching) is seizing swiftly. So Allah refuted their statement, saying: ﴿Have We not established for them a sanctuary﴾, i.e., have We not settled them in a sanctuary and made it a place for them? The meaning of ﴿secure﴾ is: a place of security in which people feel safe, because the Arabs used to raid one another, while the people of Makkah were safe within the Sanctuary from killing, captivity and raiding. I.e., how then would they fear when they embrace Islam while in a secure sanctuary?! ﴿Is brought [yujba]﴾ [Nafi' read "tujba" with a ta'], i.e., gathered to it and carried to it from [every] direction are fruits, ﴿as a provision from Us﴾, i.e., from Our presence. ﴿But most of them﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, ﴿do not know﴾ that it is Allah who did this for them, so that they would thank Him. The meaning of the verse is: When you are secure in My sanctuary, eating My provision while worshipping other than Me, how would you fear when you worship Me and believe in Me?! Then He warned them of the punishment of the earlier nations, saying: ﴿And how many a town have We destroyed which exulted in its livelihood﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "its livelihood" (ma'ishataha) is in the accusative by the omission of "fi" (in), and the meaning is: it exulted in its livelihood. Al-bata (exultation) is transgression in blessing. Ata said: They lived in exultation, so they ate Allah's provision and worshipped idols.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those are their dwellings, not inhabited after them except a little﴾. Ibn Abbas said: None dwelt in them except travelers and passersby, for a day or an hour. The meaning is: they were not inhabited after them except for a little inhabiting. ﴿And We are the inheritors﴾, i.e., none succeeded them in their dwellings after their destruction, so they remained ruins, uninhabited.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 59–61:

﴿Your Lord would never destroy the cities﴾, meaning the cities whose people are disbelievers, ﴿until He has sent in their mother [city] a messenger﴾, that is, in its greatest one. He specified the greatest for the sending of a messenger because a messenger is sent only to the nobles, and the nobles of a people are its kings, and they dwell in the places which are the "mother" of what surrounds them. Qatadah said: "Umm al-Qura (the mother of the cities) is Makkah, and the messenger is Muhammad (ﷺ)."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿who recites to them Our verses﴾. Muqatil said: the messenger informs them that the punishment will descend upon them if they do not believe.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We would never destroy the cities unless their people were wrongdoers﴾, that is, He destroyed them because of their wrongdoing. Their wrongdoing is their association of partners [with Allah]. ﴿And whatever you have been given is but the enjoyment of worldly life and its adornment﴾, that is, what you have been given of wealth and goodness, ﴿but what is with Allah is better and more lasting﴾, that is, the reward, which is better and more enduring for its people. ﴿Then will you not reason?﴾ That what remains is better than what perishes?!

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Is one to whom We have promised a good promise and who will meet it [like one who We have given the enjoyment of worldly life and then, on the Day of Resurrection, will be among those brought forward [for punishment]]?﴾ Scholars differed about who it was revealed concerning, in four opinions. The first: it was revealed concerning the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and Abu Jahl. The second: concerning Ali and Hamzah, peace be upon them, and Abu Jahl. Both opinions are narrated from Mujahid. The third: concerning the believer and the disbeliever, related by Qatadah. The fourth: concerning Ammar and al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, related by al-Suddi. Regarding the "good promise," there are two opinions: one is Paradise, and the other is victory.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and he will meet it﴾, that is, he will encounter and reach it. ﴿Like one We have given the enjoyment of worldly life﴾, that is, like one who is provided with something that perishes and passes away soon. ﴿Then, on the Day of Resurrection, he will be among those brought forward﴾: there are two opinions concerning this. One is that they will be among those brought forward into the punishment of Allah, related by Qatadah. The other is that they will be among those brought forward for recompense, related by al-Mawardi.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 28, verses 62–67:**

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And the day He calls to them﴾, meaning: Allah, the Exalted, calls to the polytheists on the Day of Resurrection, ﴿and He will say, "Where are My partners?"﴾ This is in the form of recounting their own words, and the meaning is: "Where are My partners whom you claimed?" ﴿Those upon whom the Word has come into effect will say﴾, meaning: the punishment became obligatory for them, and they are the leaders of misguidance. (p-236) There are two opinions about them. The first: they are the leaders of the polytheists. The second: they are the devils. ﴿"Our Lord, these are the ones we misled﴾, meaning the followers, ﴿we misled them as we ourselves were misled﴾, meaning: we led them astray as we were led astray. ﴿We disassociate ourselves before You﴾, meaning: we disassociate ourselves from them before You. The meaning is that some of them will disown others and they will become enemies. ﴿And it will be said﴾ to the disbelievers among the children of Adam, ﴿"Call upon your partners"﴾, meaning: seek help from your gods so that they may rescue you from the punishment. ﴿So they call upon them, but they do not respond to them﴾, meaning: they do not answer them by coming to their aid. ﴿And they will see the punishment; if only they had been guided﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the answer to "law" (if only) is omitted, and the meaning is: "If only they had been guided, they would not have followed them, and would not have seen the punishment."

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿And the day He calls to them﴾, meaning: Allah calls to the disbelievers and questions them, ﴿and He will say, "What did you answer the messengers?"﴾

﴿Then the reports will be obscured to them﴾. Abu Razin al-'Uqayli, Qatadah, Abu al-'Aliyah, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and 'Asim al-Jahdari recited: "fa-'amiyat" with a raised 'ayn (ʿamiyat as 'amiyat with damma) and a shadda on the mim. The exegetes said: the proofs were hidden from them, and they were called "anba'" (reports) because they are information that is reported. Ibn Qutaybah said: the meaning is that they were blinded to them, due to the severity of the terror, so they did not answer. The "anba'" here means the proofs.

His statement, the Exalted: ﴿So they will not question one another﴾. There are three opinions concerning this. The first: no one asks another about the proof; this was said by al-Dahhak. The second: the meaning is that they fell silent, so they do not question one another at that time; this was said by al-Farra'. The third: no one asks another to bear any part of his sins; this was related by al-Mawardi.

﴿As for him who repents﴾ from polytheism, ﴿and believes﴾, meaning: affirms the Oneness of Allah, ﴿and does righteous deeds﴾, meaning: performs the obligatory duties, ﴿then perhaps he will be among the successful﴾. The word "perhaps" (ʿasā) from Allah is binding.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verses 71–75:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Will you not then listen?﴾ That is, listening of understanding and acceptance, so that you might draw evidence from this for the Oneness of God, Exalted is He?! Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 76–78:

(p-239) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Qarun was of the people of Musa﴾, meaning: of his clan. There are three opinions regarding his lineage to Musa.

The first: he was the son of his paternal uncle (ibn 'ammihi). This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn 'Abbas, and 'Abd Allah ibn al-Harith, Ibrahim, and Ibn Jurayj also said so.

The second: he was the son of his maternal aunt (ibn khalatihi). This was narrated by 'Ata' from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: that he was the paternal uncle (amm) of Musa. This was said by Ibn Ishaq.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Qarun" is a non-Arabic proper name that is not declined (la yanṣarif). Even if it were a pattern of Arabic (fa'ul) derived from "qarantu al-shay'" (I joined the thing), it would still not be declined.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿so he oppressed them﴾ (fa-baghā 'alayhim). Regarding this there are five opinions. The first: he hired a prostitute to accuse Musa with herself, and she did so; Musa then made her swear to what she had said, and she informed him of her story, and this was his oppression. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: he oppressed by disbelief in Allah, exalted is He; this was said by al-Dahhak. The third: by arrogance; this was said by Qatada. The fourth: that he increased the length of his garments by a span (shibr); this was said by 'Ata' al-Khurasani and Shahr ibn Hawshab. The fifth: that he used to serve Pharaoh, and so he transgressed against the Children of Israel and wronged them; this was related by al-Mawardi.

(p-240) There are two opinions regarding what is meant by "its keys" (mafatihihi).

The first: they are the keys of the treasuries with which doors are opened; this was said by Mujahid and Qatada. Al-A'mash narrated from Khaythama who said: "The keys of Qarun were a load for sixty mules, and they were of leather; each key was like a finger."

The second: they are his treasuries; this was said by al-Suddi, Abu Salih, and al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj said: "This is more likely, that his keys are the treasuries of his wealth," and Ibn Qutayba went in this direction too. Abu Salih said: "His treasuries used to be carried by forty mules."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿would weigh down with the company of men﴾ (la-tanū' bil-'uṣbah), meaning: they would burden them and make them lean. The sense of the sentence is: "the company would weigh down [the keys]," but when the bā' entered upon "al-'uṣbah," the tā' took a fatḥa, as you say: "this takes away the sights" (yadhhabu bil-abṣār) and "this takes away the sights" (yudhhibu al-abṣār). This is the choice of al-Farra', Ibn Qutayba, al-Zajjaj, and others. Some said: this is from the inverted construction (maqlūb), and its estimation is: "Indeed the company would weigh down with its keys," as one says: "Indeed her buttocks weigh her down" (innahā la-tanū' bihā 'ajīzatuhā), meaning: she weighs down on her buttocks. They recited:

"I ransomed with his self my self and my wealth, and I did not spare you except what I am able to bear."

meaning: I ransomed with my self and my wealth his self. This is the choice of Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash. We have already explained the meaning of "al-'uṣbah" in Surah Yusuf (12:8), and regarding what is meant by it here there are six opinions. The first: forty men; narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: between three and ten; narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: fifteen; said by Mujahid. The fourth: above ten up to forty; said by Qatada. The fifth: seventy men; said by Abu Salih. The sixth: between fifteen and forty; related by al-Zajjaj.

(p-241) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When his people said to him﴾. Regarding the speaker to him there are two opinions. The first: they were the believers from his people; this was said by al-Suddi. The second: it was the saying of Musa to him; related by al-Mawardi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Do not exult﴾ (la tafrah). Ibn Qutayba said: the meaning is: do not be insolent (la ta'shar), and do not be overbearing (la tabtar). The poet said:

"I am not one who exults when fortune pleases me, nor one who frets at its changing turns."

meaning: I am not insolent; as for joy, it is not disliked. ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the exultant﴾. Abu Raja', Abu Hayawa, 'Asim al-Jahdari, and Ibn Abi 'Abla recited: "al-fārihīn" [with an alif].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And seek, through what Allah has given you﴾, meaning: seek through what Allah has given you of wealth. Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn al-Sumayfa recited: "wa-ittabi'" with a doubled tā', a kasra on the bā' after it, and a silent unpointed 'ayn. ﴿the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ (al-dar al-ākhirah), which is: Paradise; and this is achieved by spending it in pursuit of Allah's good pleasure and thanking the Benefactor who bestowed it. ﴿and do not forget your portion of this world﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: that you work in this world for the Hereafter; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority. The second: that you advance the surplus and keep what suffices you; this was said by al-Hasan. The third: that you be independent through the lawful from the unlawful; this was said by Qatada.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿and do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ there are three opinions related by al-Mawardi. The first: give the surplus of your wealth as He has increased it beyond your need. The second: do good in what has been made obligatory upon you, as He has done good in His favour to you. The third: do good in seeking the lawful, as He has done good to you in making it lawful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not seek corruption in the land﴾, so that you act in it with acts of disobedience.

﴿He said, "I have only been given it on account of knowledge I have." Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation? And the criminals will not be asked about their sins.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I have only been given it﴾, meaning the wealth, ﴿on account of knowledge I have﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions.

The first: on account of knowledge I have of the craft of gold; narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: "This has no basis, for alchemy is false and has no reality." The second: by the pleasure of Allah with me; said by Ibn Zayd. The third: on account of a good that Allah knows is in me; said by Muqatil. The fourth: I was given it only for the excellence of my knowledge; said by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: he claimed that he was given wealth for his knowledge of the Torah. The fifth: on account of knowledge I have of the modes of earning; related by al-Mawardi.

(p-243) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did he not know﴾, meaning Qarun, ﴿that Allah had destroyed﴾ with punishment ﴿before him of generations﴾ in the world when they denied their messengers, ﴿who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation﴾ of wealth.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾ there are three opinions. The first: they will not be asked, so that those before them may know it, even if they are questioned with a question of rebuke; this was said by al-Hasan. The second: that the angels recognize them by their marks, so they do not ask them about their sins; this was said by Mujahid. The third: they will enter the Fire without reckoning; this was said by Qatada. al-Suddi said: they will be punished and will not be asked about their sins.

Abu al-Mutawakkil and Ibn al-Sumayfa recited: "wa-ittabi'" with a doubled tā', a kasra on the bā' after it, and a silent unpointed 'ayn. ﴿the Abode of the Hereafter﴾ (al-dar al-ākhirah), which is: Paradise; and this is achieved by spending it in pursuit of Allah's good pleasure and thanking the Benefactor who bestowed it. ﴿and do not forget your portion of this world﴾. Regarding this there are three opinions. The first: that you work in this world for the Hereafter; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and the majority. The second: that you advance the surplus and keep what suffices you; this was said by al-Hasan. The third: that you be independent through the lawful from the unlawful; this was said by Qatada.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿and do good as Allah has done good to you﴾ there are three opinions related by al-Mawardi. The first: give the surplus of your wealth as He has increased it beyond your need. The second: do good in what has been made obligatory upon you, as He has done good in His favour to you. The third: do good in seeking the lawful, as He has done good to you in making it lawful.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and do not seek corruption in the land﴾, so that you act in it with acts of disobedience.

﴿He said, "I have only been given it on account of knowledge I have." Did he not know that Allah had destroyed before him generations who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation? And the criminals will not be asked about their sins.﴾

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿I have only been given it﴾, meaning the wealth, ﴿on account of knowledge I have﴾. Regarding this there are five opinions.

The first: on account of knowledge I have of the craft of gold; narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. Al-Zajjaj said: "This has no basis, for alchemy is false and has no reality." The second: by the pleasure of Allah with me; said by Ibn Zayd. The third: on account of a good that Allah knows is in me; said by Muqatil. The fourth: I was given it only for the excellence of my knowledge; said by al-Farra'. Al-Zajjaj said: he claimed that he was given wealth for his knowledge of the Torah. The fifth: on account of knowledge I have of the modes of earning; related by al-Mawardi.

(p-243) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Did he not know﴾, meaning Qarun, ﴿that Allah had destroyed﴾ with punishment ﴿before him of generations﴾ in the world when they denied their messengers, ﴿who were greater than him in strength and more abundant in accumulation﴾ of wealth.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And the criminals will not be asked about their sins﴾ there are three opinions. The first: they will not be asked, so that those before them may know it, even if they are questioned with a question of rebuke; this was said by al-Hasan. The second: that the angels recognize them by their marks, so they do not ask them about their sins; this was said by Mujahid. The third: they will enter the Fire without reckoning; this was said by Qatada. al-Suddi said: they will be punished and will not be asked about their sins.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 79–80:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So he went out to his people in his adornment.﴾ Al-Hasan said: "In red and yellow garments." ʿIkrimah said: "In garments dyed with safflower (ʿuṣfur)." Wahb ibn Munabbih said: "He went out on a grey-white mule, upon which was a red saddle of urjuwan (crimson silk), and with him were four thousand fighting men, and three hundred maidservants adorned with jewelry and finery, upon white mules." Al-Zajjaj said: "Al-urjuwan, in the language, is a red dye."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he is one of great fortune.﴾ That is, he is one who possesses a abundant share of worldly life.

[And His saying]: ﴿But those who had been given knowledge said: "Woe to you! The reward of Allah is better for one who believes and does righteousness."﴾ Ibn ʿAbbas said: "They mean the rabbis (aḥbār) of the Children of Israel." Muqatil said: "Those who had been given knowledge of what Allah promised in the Hereafter said to those who wished for what Qarun had been given: ﴿Woe to you! The reward of Allah﴾, that is, what is with Him of recompense, ﴿is better for one who believes﴾ than what Qarun was given."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But none receives it except the patient.﴾ Abu ʿUbaydah said: "None is granted success in it and is provided with it." Ubayy ibn Kaʿb and Ibn Abi ʿAblah read: "wa-lā yalaqqāhā" with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, a sukūn on the lām, and a lightened qāf. Regarding the referent of "it" (hā), there are three opinions.

One: that it refers to righteous deeds; this was said by Muqatil. The second: that it refers to Paradise, and the meaning is: none is given it in the Hereafter except those who are patient in obeying Allah; this was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib. The third: that it refers to the statement they uttered, which is their saying: ﴿The reward of Allah is better﴾; this was said by al-Farra'.
