(p. 245) Allah's words: ﴿So We caused the earth to swallow him and his home.﴾ When Qarun persisted in his insolence by slandering Musa, as its explanation has already been given [al-Qasas: 76], Musa became angry and invoked Allah against him. Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "I have commanded the earth to obey you, so command it." Musa said: "O earth, seize him!" It seized him until it had swallowed his couch. When Musa saw this, he appealed to it by the ties of kinship, saying: "Seize him!" It seized him until it had swallowed his feet. He kept saying, "Seize him!" until it had swallowed him entirely. Then Allah the Exalted revealed to him: "O Musa, how harsh you are! By My might and My majesty, if he had called upon Me for help, I would have helped him." Ibn Abbas said: "He was made to sink into the earth down to the lowest earth." Samura ibn Jundub said: "He is made to sink a man's height every day, and he will reach the lowest earth on the Day of Resurrection." Muqatil said: "When Qarun perished, the Children of Israel said: 'Musa only destroyed him so that he could take his wealth and his home.' So Allah caused his home and his wealth to sink into the earth three days after him."

Allah's words: ﴿They had no group to help them against Allah﴾, that is, to protect him from Allah. ﴿Nor was he among those who could defend themselves﴾, that is, among those who could ward off what had befallen him. Then Allah informed us that those who had wished to be in his place regretted that wish, by means of the verse that follows this one.

(p. 246) As for His words ﴿Had Allah not been gracious to us, He would have caused the earth to swallow us﴾: most readers recite the first letter with a ḍamma and the sīn with a kasra (*khasafa*). Yaʿqub, al-Walid from Ibn Amir, Hafs, and Aban from Asim read both the khāʾ and the sīn with a fatḥa (*khasafa* as *khasafa*, i.e. "khasafa" read in the active form with fatḥa on both).

As for His words *wa-ykaʾ* (ويك): Ibn Abbas said its meaning is "Have you not seen?" Abu Ubayda and al-Kisa'i said the same. Al-Farra' said: "*Wayka anna*" in the speech of the Arabs is a confirmation, like a man saying, "Do you not see the handiwork and kindness of Allah?" One of them recited to me:

*Wayka anna man yakun lahu nashabun yuhabb, wa-man yaftaqir yaʿish ʿaysha ḍurr*
Do you not see that whoever has wealth is loved, and whoever is poor lives a life of hardship?

Ibn al-Anbari said: regarding His words ﴿And it is as if Allah...﴾ (*wayka-annahu*), there are three possible interpretations.

If you wish, you may say that *wayka* is one particle and *annahu* is another particle, and the meaning is: "Have you not seen that he...?" The evidence for this is the saying of the poet:

*Salatani al-ṭalaq an raatani, qall mali, qad jiʾtumani bi-nukr*
*Wayka anna man yakun lahu nashabb yuhabb, wa-man yaftaqir yaʿish ʿaysha ḍurr*

(The two of them asked me for divorce when they saw me, saying that my wealth had dwindled, and that you had come to me with something strange. Do you not see that whoever has wealth is loved, and whoever is poor lives a life of hardship?)

The second interpretation: *wayka* is a particle and *annahu* is a particle, and the meaning is: "Woe to you, I know that he..." The lām has been deleted, as they say *qum la abā laka* ("stand, may you have no father"), meaning *la abā laka*. They also recited:

*Abil-mawti alladhi la budda anni, mulaqin la abāki tukhawwifīni*
Is it by death, which I must surely meet, that you frighten me, may you have no father?

He meant *la abā laki*, and deleted the lām.

The third interpretation: *wayy* is a particle and *kaʾannahu* is a particle, so the meaning of *wayy* is wonder (*taʿajjub*), as you say, "Wayy, why did you do such-and-such?" The meaning of *ka-annahu* is "I think it and know it," as you say in speech, "It is as if you see relief has come," meaning: "I think relief is coming." They joined the *yāʾ* to the *kāf* in His words ﴿*wayka-annahu*﴾ because the two were frequently used together, just as they made *yā ibna umma* in the Muṣḥaf a single letter, though it is two letters. Some of them, including Yaʿqub, pause on *wayka* in both places and begin with *anna* and *annahu* in both places. Al-Zajjaj reported from al-Khalil that he said: *wayy* is separated from *ka-anna*, because the people expressed regret and said *wayy*, regretting what had passed from them. Everyone who regrets and shows his regret says *wayy*. Ibn Qutayba related from some scholars that he said: the meaning of *wayka-anna* is "mercy upon you" in the dialect of Himyar.

His words ﴿Had Allah not been gracious to us﴾, that is, with mercy, well-being, and faith, ﴿He would have caused the earth to swallow us﴾.

(p-248) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That is the Last Abode﴾ meaning Paradise, ﴿We assign it to those who do not desire exaltation upon the earth﴾. On this there are five opinions. The first: it is arrogance (al-baghy), said by Sa'id ibn Jubayr. The second: nobility and honour (al-sharaf wal-izz), said by al-Hasan. The third: oppression (al-zulm), said by al-Dahhak. The fourth: polytheism (al-shirk), said by Yahya ibn Salam. The fifth: pride (al-istikbar) in refusing faith, said by Muqatil.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Nor corruption﴾. On this there are two opinions. One: acting in acts of disobedience (al-ma'asi), said by Ikrimah. The second: calling to other than the worship of Allah, said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the good end is for the God-fearing﴾, that is, the praiseworthy end is theirs.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Whoever comes with a good deed﴾. We have explained it in Surah al-Naml (27:89).

He means those who associated partners (with Allah), ﴿except what they used to do﴾, that is, except the recompense of their deeds of polytheism, and its recompense is the Fire.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 28, verse 85–88:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an for you﴾. Muqatil said: "The Messenger of Allah ﷺ left the cave at night and set off in the direction of Madinah, travelling by a route other than the usual one out of fear of pursuit. When he felt safe, he returned to the road and stopped at al-Juhfah, between Makkah and Madinah. He recognised the road to Makkah and longed for it, and he remembered his birthplace. Jibril came to him and said: 'Do you long for your land and your birthplace?' He said: 'Yes.' He said: 'Indeed Allah, Exalted is He, says: ﴿Indeed, He who has ordained the Qur'an for you will surely bring you back to a return﴾.' So this verse was revealed at al-Juhfah."

Regarding the meaning of ﴿ordained for you﴾ there are three views. The first: the obligation to act upon the Qur'an was imposed upon you; this was said by ʿAṭāʾ ibn Abī Rabah and Ibn Qutaybah. The second: He gave you the Qur'an; this was said by Mujahid. The third: He sent down the Qur'an to you; this was said by Muqatil, al-Farra', and Abu ʿUbaydah.

Regarding His saying ﴿will surely bring you back to a return﴾ there are four views.

The first: to Makkah. This was narrated by al-ʿAwfi from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid in one narration and al-Dahhak also said so. Ibn Qutaybah said: the *maʿad* (return) of a man is his homeland, because he travels through the lands and roams the earth and then returns to his homeland.

The second: to your return (*maʿād*) of Paradise. This was narrated by ʿIkrimah from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Hasan and al-Zuhri also said so. If it is objected that "return" implies that he had been in that place before, then there are three answers. The first: since his father Adam was in Paradise and then was brought out, it was as if his offspring had been brought out of it; so when he enters it, it is as if he has been restored. The second: he entered it on the night of the Mi'raj, so when he enters it on the Day of Resurrection, it is a return to it. Ibn Jarir mentioned both of these. The third: the Arabs say "the matter returned to such-and-such," even if it never had any existence in it at all, and they recited:

"And the man is only like the shooting star and its light, which turns to ash after it was blazing."

We have explained this in His saying: ﴿And to Allah all matters are returned﴾ [al-Baqarah: 210].

The third: it means He will bring you back to death. This was narrated by Sa'id ibn Jubayr from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Abu Sa'id al-Khudri also said so.

The fourth: He will bring you back to the Resurrection through resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan, al-Zuhri, Mujahid in one narration, and al-Zajjaj.

Then He began a statement by which He responds to the disbelievers when they attributed misguidance to the Prophet ﷺ, so He said: ﴿Say: My Lord knows best who has come with guidance﴾. The meaning is: He knows that I have come with guidance, and that you are in manifest error. Then He reminded him of His blessings, so He said: ﴿And you did not expect that the Book would be bestowed upon you﴾, that is, that you would be a prophet and that the Qur'an would be revealed to you, ﴿except as a mercy from your Lord﴾. Al-Farra' said: this is a disconnected exception (*istithnāʾ munqaṭiʿ*), and the meaning is: but your Lord has shown you mercy, so He sent it down to you. ﴿So never be a supporter of the disbelievers﴾, that is, a helper to them in their religion. This is because they invited him to the religion of his forefathers, so he was commanded to guard against them. The address in this and similar verses is to him, while the intended audience is the people of his religion, lest they back the disbelievers or agree with them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Everything will perish except His face﴾. There are two views regarding this.

One: except what is sought by it His face; this was narrated by ʿAṭāʾ from Ibn ʿAbbas, and al-Thawri also said so. The second: except Him; this was said by al-Dahhak and Abu ʿUbaydah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿To Him belongs the judgment﴾, that is, the decision among the creatures in the Hereafter, to the exclusion of any other. ﴿And to Him you will be returned﴾ in the Hereafter.
